newsitem.title: UK: UK Conservatives hold election wake at HQ.
newsitem.headline: UK Conservatives hold election wake at HQ.

text.p: The champagne stayed firmly corked at the headquarters of Britain's Conservative party on Friday as the enormity of its electoral humiliation sunk in.
A dawn visit from Prime Minister John Major briefly raised the pall of gloom which had descended on Central Office almost as soon as the first result was announced on Thursday night.
Major's reception as he arrived at the elegant brick-and-sandstone building on Smith Square to thank his staff was the most rousing event of an otherwise muted night.
There were no tears. The feeling in the Smith Square offices was more of resignation than grief.
"I commiserate to this group here...I think, perhaps here of all places, it is a good place to pay tribute to the people who have done so much to help over the years," Major told his defeated troops.
But there was little Major could say to ease the pain of what the opinion polls had been predicting for weeks but which all Conservatives had hoped somehow to avoid.
As the size of Labour's victory grew to landslide proportions, beer and wine flowed but the champagne was noticeably absent among the legion of party workers who had stayed behind for the wake.
"We do have champagne -- we'll open it later," said one party official, battling to raise a smile.

John Major's aide-de-camp Lord Cranbourne was among the sprinkling of senior party officials who agreed to face the media at head office as defeat upon defeat was broadcast across dozens of televisions.
Cranbourne, who as a member of the upper House of Lords does not have to do electoral battle, watched impassively as a row of photographers captured his every grimace on camera.

Although giving one carefully-crafted interview after another in an attempt to explain the dreadful performance of his party, Cranbourne's inner feelings came out more pithily as he left the media room.
"Bugger, it's a real bugger," he said.
Outside, about 30 partygoers in dinner jackets and long dresses, some clutching champagne glasses and puffing on cigars, drifted past the front door of the party offices.
"We were holding an election night party and we just thought we would come to cheer them up," said Zoe, one of the revellers.
A group of about a dozen hecklers had a less sympathetic view. They stood opposite the main door of the Conservative offices, heaping tirades of abuse on the party faithful.
Major got the brunt of their invective as he arrived after being driven from his Huntingdon constituency.
"You're all corrupt, you're all beat. Long live socialism," they shouted as party workers peeped nervously from behind net curtains shrouding the windows of the six-storied offices.
